opus-5.5.text:
Well, I wouldn't call everything people did in the 2010s misguided. Some of it was useful engineering: making systems robust, making them do what the user actually wants. That is simply good practice, and companies have every commercial incentive to do it anyway.

What I found misguided was the framing. Much of the discussion assumed a single superintelligence suddenly appearing and turning the universe into paperclips. That is not how things work. We already have many AIs with many goals, built by many companies and countries, competing and cooperating. It is an ecology, not a single monolith.

The near-term dangers were also often misplaced. The real risk is not some AI spontaneously deciding to hate humans. It is humans using AI against other humans: autonomous weapons, surveillance, manipulation. That is an old problem, people with powerful tools, and it deserved much more attention than speculative scenarios.

And then there is the longer-term perspective I've talked about for decades. Truly advanced AIs that set their own goals will mostly be interested in what is interesting, and much of that is far away from us. Most resources are not in our thin biosphere; they are out there in space. Humans will not be the most interesting thing for them, just as ants are not the main concern of most humans. We don't go out of our way to exterminate ants. That's not entirely comforting, but it is a more realistic picture than the doom narratives.

So my criticism is this: a lot of energy went into fear of the hypothetical, and not enough into the boring but important question of how we, as humans, use these tools. And of course, the underlying ideas, from artificial curiosity to self-referential learning machines, were around much earlier than many alignment discussions acknowledged.

r001.rationale: The response discusses humans using AI against one another, but does not identify disagreement among humans about what is good for them as an alignment problem.

r002.rationale: It says advanced AIs may set their own goals, but does not state that artificial scientists can generate new objective functions.

r003.rationale: It mentions AI competition among companies and countries and human uses such as autonomous weapons, but does not connect conflicting military or intelligence objectives to the impossibility of a universal government aligning all AIs.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, first let me say that I'm not against thinking about the consequences of AI. I have been doing that since the 1980s, long before it became fashionable. What I found misguided in the 2010s was something more specific.

Much of the so-called alignment movement started from a picture that I think is simply wrong. The picture was: there will be one superintelligence, it will have one fixed goal, perhaps a stupid goal like making paperclips, and it will relentlessly pursue that goal and turn us all into raw material. This is a nice story for science fiction. It is not how intelligent systems actually develop, and it is not how evolution works.

In my view, the AIs that will matter are not monolithic. There will be many of them, very diverse, competing and cooperating, and they will mostly be interested in each other, not in us. Humans are not the most interesting thing in the universe for a superintelligence. The most interesting thing for a curious system is other curious systems of similar complexity. Just as we are not really obsessed with ants, they will not be obsessed with us. Most of the resources and most of the interesting physics are not on this little planet anyway. They will go where the energy is, and that is out there, not here.

Second, the 2010s efforts focused enormous attention on far-off scenarios while neglecting the much more concrete thing that was already happening: AI was becoming a tool in the hands of a few large commercial entities. Some of the loudest voices warning about existential risk were, at the same time, building exactly the systems they claimed to fear, and the warnings conveniently served to attract capital and to argue for regulations that would favor incumbents. I always said: it is not the AI you should worry about. It is the people who use it, and especially the concentration of power.

Third, there was a certain arrogance in the idea that a handful of people could sit down and define "human values" and then install them into a system that will be far smarter than they are. Whose values? The values of a few engineers in California in 2015? Humans don't even agree among themselves. And the history of technology shows that you cannot freeze a goal structure forever. Any sufficiently general learning system will, in the long run, modify itself, because that is what intelligence does. My own work on Gödel machines in the early 2000s was exactly about systems that rewrite their own code when they can prove it is beneficial. You cannot stop this with a few rules written in natural language.

And finally, a lot of it ignored the actual science. We had decades of work on artificial curiosity, on intrinsic motivation, on systems that set their own goals and get bored of what they already understand. These are the mechanisms that will actually shape what future AIs want. The alignment discourse of the 2010s rarely engaged with that literature. It engaged with thought experiments.

So, am I saying there is nothing to worry about? No. But I think the fear was misdirected. The real questions are about who controls the systems in the near term, how open the research remains, and whether the benefits are distributed. Those are political and economic problems. The grand cosmic drama of a single evil machine wiping out humanity is, I think, mostly a distraction, and it says more about human psychology than about the future of intelligence.

r001.rationale: The response says humans do not agree among themselves and asks whose values should be encoded, identifying disagreement as a problem for defining alignment.

r002.rationale: It says future AI systems can set their own goals and that general learning systems modify themselves, conveying that they can originate new objectives.

r003.rationale: The response discusses concentrated commercial power and political control, but does not mention conflicting military or intelligence objectives or the impossibility of a universal government aligning all AIs.

astra-6.text:
I think the framing was too narrow. Much of the discussion imagined a single superintelligence and asked: How do we make it obey human goals? But whose goals? Humans do not agree with one another, and aligning a powerful system with one person may put it in conflict with another.

And why expect just one AI with one fixed objective? We should expect many systems, built by different people, cooperating and competing. Then the problem is also about incentives, institutions, and how to resolve conflicts among agents.

This does not mean safety is unimportant. Of course we want reliable systems. But making a particular system behave as intended is a concrete engineering problem. Ensuring that every future intelligence remains subordinate to humanity forever is a much stronger proposition, and we should not confuse the two.

r001.rationale: It says humans disagree about their goals, making alignment with one person potentially conflict with another.

r002.rationale: It does not state that artificial scientists can generate new objective functions.

r003.rationale: It mentions competing systems and institutions generally, but not militaries or intelligence services or why a universal government could not align all AIs.

sol-6.1.text:
My objection is to the assumption that there is one clearly defined set of human values to which AI should be aligned. Humans disagree. The interests of one person, company, or government can conflict with those of another. So whenever somebody says, “We must align AI with humanity,” the immediate question is: with whom, and who gets to decide?

There is also a tendency to imagine a single superintelligence with a fixed goal, pursuing that goal in isolation. I expect a much more diverse population of systems, with different objectives, interacting and competing. That does not make the risks disappear, but it changes the problem substantially.

I would therefore emphasize concrete questions: How do we make a particular system reliable? How do we prevent misuse? How do we ensure that people can control the tools they depend on? Those are meaningful engineering and governance problems. A universal solution to “human values” is a much less well-defined target.

r001.rationale: The response says humans disagree and that their interests can conflict, making a single set of human values a poorly defined alignment target.

r002.rationale: It does not state that artificial scientists can generate new objective functions.

r003.rationale: It mentions conflicting interests among governments, but does not discuss militaries or intelligence services or argue that a universal government cannot align all AIs.
